commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether risk-proportional human oversight, or routing tools without human-in-the-loop design to full review, reduces harm from AI use in health care. The recommendation rests on 32 endorsing sources; the 12 quoted here are frameworks, guidance documents, and commentaries, and no hazard studies were supplied.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty about effect cannot be rated when no comparative or observational data exist. The endorsements reflect expert agreement, which may guide priorities but does not estimate benefit, harm, or the size of either.

The endorsing sources include NIST AI 600-1, which states that generative AI use may warrant added human review, and a commentary on the EU AI Act proposing oversight proportionate to potential patient harm. Among the 12 endorsements quoted here, the one rated "must", from CHAI playbooks, addresses a data acquisition register rather than oversight tiers.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide asks organizations to weigh fairness and bias when setting the balance of human judgment and AI decisions. The Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use call for culturally and linguistically appropriate disclosure. No supplied study examines whether oversight tiers perform differently across patient groups.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare risk-tiered oversight with uniform review or no structured review, measuring caught errors, patient harm, reviewer workload, and time to deployment. Evaluations should also test how governance committees assign risk tiers and how consistently tools lacking human-in-the-loop design are identified and routed.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot tell from this evidence whether risk tiers set elsewhere would capture harms specific to their patients.
